title: 3-Read Friday #131
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton's 3-Read Friday #131 curates three blog posts, each with a short editorial gloss. The first, by Adam Boxer, argues that copying from the board achieves close to nothing cognitively while eating lesson time, takes on the usual pushbacks of revision, inspection and evidence of learning, and proposes what students should do instead. Barton jokes that it echoes his own earlier "Myth of Copying Things Down" post. The second, by Ben Rodgers, describes two years of tinkering with curriculum booklets, which shifted his time from creating resources to thinking hard about how to teach them, and offers a four-part structure and candid warnings about where booklets go wrong. The third, by Michael Slavinsky, argues that nearly any traditional homework task can now be bypassed by AI in seconds and outlines three ways to set homework that cannot easily be gamed, each with trade-offs. Pass B: the Boxer piece is already in the archive; the Rodgers and Slavinsky links could not be resolved from the email.
points: Copying from the board consumes time and fractures the flow of a lesson while engaging students' thinking very little, according to the Boxer post Barton highlights.
Booklets are valued less as handouts than as a prompt for intellectual preparation, moving teacher time from making materials to planning how to teach them.
Barton notes that schools using maths booklets showed consistent lesson quality, but Rodgers is open about where booklets can fail.
Slavinsky's argument is that ticking off AI-completed homework teaches nothing, so homework design must change rather than rely on detection.
Barton's own June 2025 position, that maths homework is dead as an assessment tool, frames this week's three reads as a coherent theme about where student thinking should happen.
